papers.title: Mitochondrial membrane remodeling in stress adaptation: Lipid control of organelle quality.
papers.summary: This paper discusses how mitochondria remodel their lipid membranes as a way to adapt to cellular stress. It focuses on how changes in lipid composition help maintain mitochondrial quality control, influencing processes like fusion, fission, and degradation. The work highlights lipids as active regulators of organelle health rather than passive structural components.
papers.why: Lipid-driven mitochondrial membrane remodeling is directly relevant to understanding mitophagy regulation in neurons, a core mechanism this PhD project investigates alongside spatial metabolomic changes in brain tissue.

papers.title: Targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome in Alzheimer's disease: Mechanistic insights and therapeutic advances.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how the NLRP3 inflammasome, a protein complex involved in inflammatory signaling, contributes to Alzheimer's disease progression. It discusses the molecular mechanisms by which NLRP3 activation drives neuroinflammation, amyloid and tau pathology. The paper also covers emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at blocking NLRP3 to slow disease progression.
papers.why: While focused on neuroinflammation rather than mitophagy directly, NLRP3 activation is tightly linked to mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitophagy, offering mechanistic context relevant to neuronal autophagy research in neurodegeneration.

papers.title: The Microbiome-Mitochondria Axis in aging: a self-reinforcing vicious cycle linking metabolic dysregulation, mitochondrial quality control failure, and inflammaging.
papers.summary: This paper proposes that gut microbiome imbalance and mitochondrial dysfunction reinforce each other over the aging process, creating a vicious cycle. As mitochondrial quality control fails, cells accumulate damaged mitochondria, which triggers chronic low-grade inflammation known as inflammaging. This inflammation and metabolic dysregulation in turn worsen microbiome health, further impairing mitochondrial function and perpetuating the cycle.
papers.why: Understanding how failures in mitochondrial quality control (mitophagy) connect to systemic inflammation and metabolic dysregulation provides broader context for interpreting neuronal mitophagy defects in aging brains, relevant to interneuron and perineuronal net vulnerability.
papers.figure: A schematic diagram illustrating the proposed feedback loop between microbiome dysbiosis, mitochondrial quality control failure, and inflammaging.

papers.title: Targeted Restoration of Mitophagy Reinvigorates Aged Hematopoietic Stem Cells.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how aged hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) lose function over time, partly due to declining mitophagy, the process that clears damaged mitochondria. The researchers show that specifically restoring mitophagy in these aged stem cells can reverse some hallmarks of aging and improve their regenerative capacity. This suggests mitophagy is a targetable mechanism for rejuvenating aged stem cell populations.
papers.why: Although focused on blood stem cells rather than neurons, this paper demonstrates a direct causal link between restoring mitophagy and reversing cellular aging phenotypes, offering a conceptual and mechanistic framework potentially transferable to studies of mitophagy decline in aging neurons and interneurons.

papers.title: Crosstalk between mitophagy and metabolism in cancer: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, is linked to metabolic reprogramming in cancer cells. It discusses the molecular mechanisms connecting mitochondrial quality control to nutrient and energy pathways that tumors exploit. The review also highlights potential therapeutic strategies that target this crosstalk to treat cancer.
papers.why: Although focused on cancer, this paper could offer mechanistic insights into mitophagy-metabolism crosstalk that may translate to understanding mitochondrial quality control in neurons and interneurons.

papers.title: The white spot syndrome virus wsv156 protein hijacks Parkin-dependent mitophagy to promote viral infection.
papers.summary: This paper studies white spot syndrome virus (WSSV), a pathogen that infects shrimp, and shows that a viral protein called wsv156 manipulates the host cell's mitophagy machinery. Mitophagy is the process cells use to selectively degrade damaged mitochondria via the Parkin pathway. The researchers found that wsv156 hijacks this Parkin-dependent mitophagy process in a way that benefits the virus and promotes infection.
papers.why: Although this paper examines Parkin-dependent mitophagy mechanisms relevant conceptually to the project's focus, it is in an invertebrate viral infection model (shrimp) with no connection to neurons, brain tissue, spatial omics, or perineuronal nets.

papers.title: Asiaticoside attenuates endothelial cells senescence in diabetic retinopathy via CCND1-mediated mitophagy through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway.
papers.summary: This study looked at how a natural compound called asiaticoside affects aging (senescence) in the endothelial cells that line blood vessels in the eye, specifically in the context of diabetic retinopathy. The researchers found that asiaticoside helps reduce cellular senescence by promoting mitophagy, a process where damaged mitochondria are cleared away. This effect appears to work through a specific protein called CCND1 and a well-known signaling pathway (PI3K/AKT/mTOR) that regulates cell growth and survival.
papers.why: While focused on retinal blood vessels rather than neurons, this paper offers relevant mechanistic insight into CCND1-mediated mitophagy regulation via the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, a pathway also implicated in neuronal mitophagy and autophagy dysregulation.

papers.title: The role of the HB-EGF-regulated EGFR-mitophagy axis in maintaining cartilage homeostasis and osteoarthritis.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how a signaling molecule called HB-EGF regulates the EGFR receptor to control mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, in cartilage cells. The researchers show that this HB-EGF-EGFR-mitophagy pathway is important for maintaining healthy cartilage tissue. Disruption of this axis appears to contribute to osteoarthritis, a degenerative joint disease.
papers.why: While this study focuses on cartilage rather than neurons, it explores mitophagy regulation mechanisms that could offer mechanistic insights transferable to understanding mitophagy dysregulation in neurons and brain tissue homeostasis.
